tagline: The Red Road went black in 2000. The name stayed.
intro: Route 137 follows about 15 miles of the southeast coast of the Big Island between Kapoho and Kalapana, through lava fields. The byway's 2015 plan described huge mango trees and tree tunnels of kamani and java plum, with coconut palms and ironwoods. One old-timer suggested the mangoes along the old Kaueleau Trail were the leavings of sugar workers who ate them on the walk to and from the train.

For decades the road was paved with red volcanic cinder. Most of it went to black asphalt in 2000, and nobody changed the name. The lava keeps its own edits: in 2018 a flow buried the stretch between Kamaili Road and Pohoiki Road and cut more of it near Kapoho.

moments.title: Kapoho
moments.text: Lava buried the town in 1960, people rebuilt it with homes and vacation rentals, and in 2018 the lava came back and filled in the bay.

moments.title: MacKenzie State Recreation Area
moments.text: Ranger Albert J. MacKenzie planted ironwoods here in the 1930s above lava cliffs and ocean caves on the old King's Highway, and the park closed in May 2018 as lava came near.

moments.title: Kalapana
moments.text: The 1990 flow destroyed most of the town, buried neighboring Kaimū Bay under more than 50 feet of lava and made a new coastline, where a new black sand beach formed.
